concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual reality system
concepts.definition: A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

A system is a virtual reality (VR) system if it satisfies all three characteristics of a VR system—virtual environment, immersive experience through sensory organs, and interaction—and it is not a VR system if it does not satisfy at least one of them.

A computer-aided design (CAD) system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it supports a virtual environment and interaction, it does not support an immersive experience, since the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

A video conferencing system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it is interactive, it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience, since it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen and the user remains in the real world, with the screen only aiding interaction.

A three-dimensional (3D) movie experience is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it is not interactive, as the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.
A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

In a complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, the organism component, which typically refers to the human user, is equally important to account for as the VR hardware component and cannot be omitted because the user is always present.
The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

The surrounding physical environment is considered part of the virtual reality (VR) system because the user may respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, and may not be completely detached from the real world, so the environment may affect the user's behavior while interacting with the virtual world.

concepts.name: non-immersive virtual reality system
concepts.definition: A Non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

defining_facts.text: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world.

Non-immersive virtual reality (VR) includes specifically gaming applications, such as games on PlayStation, Xbox, or similar systems and games like World of Warcraft or similar games, that rely on computer or video game console displays and input devices such as keyboards, mice, and handheld controllers.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

concepts.name: stereoscopic vision
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.

defining_facts.text: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

never_defined.name: hardware
never_defined.definition: Hardware is a part of an extended reality (XR) system, including input devices, output devices, processing devices, central processing units, graphics processing units, and memory.

never_defined.name: virtual reality application
never_defined.definition: A Virtual reality application is an immersive application that involves creating a virtual environment, rendering a stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

never_defined.name: virtual reality display
never_defined.definition: A virtual reality display is a display, such as a head-mounted display.

never_defined.name: display resolution
never_defined.definition: Display resolution is a hardware display quality, specified in pixels, that affects visual perception, immersion, and cybersickness, with higher values reducing cybersickness only up to a point.

never_defined.name: symptom
never_defined.definition: Symptom is one of the possible signs whose occurrence during a virtual reality experience may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

never_defined.name: nausea
never_defined.definition: Nausea is a common symptom that may indicate cybersickness and is one of the scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire.

never_defined.name: headache
never_defined.definition: Headache is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

never_defined.name: excessive sweating
never_defined.definition: Excessive sweating is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

never_defined.name: dryness of mouth
never_defined.definition: Dryness of mouth is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

never_defined.name: fullness of stomach
never_defined.definition: Fullness of stomach is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

never_defined.name: vomiting
never_defined.definition: Vomiting is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself during a virtual reality experience.

never_defined.name: dizziness
never_defined.definition: Dizziness is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness or cybersickness itself.

never_defined.name: disorientation
never_defined.definition: Disorientation is a common symptom of cybersickness and one of the scores considered in the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ).

never_defined.name: fatigue
never_defined.definition: Fatigue is one of the common symptoms that may indicate the onset of cybersickness during a virtual reality experience, and may occur when hands are held in front of a device's sensor or camera.

never_defined.name: hand-eye coordination
never_defined.definition: Hand-eye coordination is a form of coordination in VR that can be disrupted as a cybersickness symptom and may require tracking and matched motion of body parts.

never_defined.name: acceptability
never_defined.definition: Acceptability is an aspect of virtual reality systems for which reducing the impact of cybersickness is important, because it makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

never_defined.name: user experience
never_defined.definition: User experience is a key concern in virtual reality system design that is enhanced by reducing cybersickness, affected by presence, and supported by wayfinding and environment design.

never_defined.name: age
never_defined.definition: Age is an internal factor for cyber sickness, and its relationship to cyber sickness susceptibility is clearer for controllable content than for general virtual reality content.

never_defined.name: gender
never_defined.definition: Gender is one of the internal factors for cyber sickness, and the effect of gender on cyber sickness is not conclusive.

never_defined.name: motion sickness susceptibility
never_defined.definition: Motion sickness susceptibility is one of the internal factors for cyber sickness, which are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: physical condition
never_defined.definition: Physical condition is one of the internal factors for cybersickness, which are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: emotional condition
never_defined.definition: Emotional condition is an internal factor for cybersickness that can increase the likelihood of experiencing it, and negative emotions at the time of use, such as anxiety, stress, or frustration, are typically associated with cybersickness.

never_defined.name: cyber sickness susceptibility
never_defined.definition: Cyber sickness susceptibility is a user's susceptibility to cyber sickness that is related to age, motion sickness susceptibility, retinal eccentricity, and physical position, and can be measured with questionnaires.

never_defined.name: controllable content
never_defined.definition: Controllable content is content for which, unlike general virtual reality (VR) content, age may be a factor in cyber sickness, making the age relationship clearer.

never_defined.name: inter-pupillary distance
never_defined.definition: Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is a factor in head-mounted display fit that determines stereoscopic vision.

never_defined.name: inter-pupillary distance fit
never_defined.definition: Inter-pupillary distance fit is a possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display users, because inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit.

never_defined.name: inter-pupillary distance adjustable range
never_defined.definition: Inter-pupillary distance adjustable range is the range of inter-pupillary distance fit in virtual reality displays, and a wider range is suggested for female users.

never_defined.name: cyber sickness risk
never_defined.definition: Cyber sickness risk is a risk that is positively correlated with motion sickness susceptibility, so higher motion sickness susceptibility is associated with more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

never_defined.name: cyber sickness symptoms
never_defined.definition: Cyber sickness symptoms are symptoms that may be more severe in individuals with higher motion sickness susceptibility or neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis.

never_defined.name: prior exposure to virtual reality systems
never_defined.definition: Prior exposure to virtual reality systems is one of the conditions that can reduce the effect of motion sickness susceptibility on cybersickness and reduce cybersickness severity over time.

never_defined.name: repeated exposure to virtual reality
never_defined.definition: Repeated exposure to virtual reality is one of the conditions that can reduce the effect of motion sickness susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time.

never_defined.name: cybersickness severity
never_defined.definition: Cybersickness severity is the level of cybersickness that postural sway can indicate and that self-report scores or ratings, machine-learning classification labels, or sickness scores can assess or quantify.

never_defined.name: sleep quality
never_defined.definition: Sleep quality is a condition that, when poor, can affect body awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: retinal eccentricity
never_defined.definition: Retinal eccentricity is a property that, when greater, may make people more susceptible to cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: neurological condition
never_defined.definition: A neurological condition is a condition, such as multiple sclerosis, in which individuals may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

never_defined.name: multiple sclerosis
never_defined.definition: Multiple sclerosis is a neurological condition that may be associated with more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

never_defined.name: standing posture
never_defined.definition: Standing posture is a user's physical position while using a virtual reality system that is likely to induce more, or more severe, cyber sickness than sitting.

never_defined.name: anxiety
never_defined.definition: Anxiety is a negative emotion that is typically associated with an increased likelihood of cybersickness and can be reduced by consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in system design.

never_defined.name: stress
never_defined.definition: Stress is a negative emotion that is typically associated with cyber sickness and can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: frustration
never_defined.definition: Frustration is a negative emotion that is typically associated with cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: personality trait
never_defined.definition: A personality trait is a trait, such as neuroticism, that may increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: neuroticism
never_defined.definition: Neuroticism is a personality trait that may increase the likelihood of cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: display type
never_defined.definition: Display type is an external hardware factor, the type of display used by the user, that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: conventional monitor
never_defined.definition: A conventional monitor is a display type other than head-mounted displays or virtual reality headset displays.

never_defined.name: stereoscopic three-dimensional video
never_defined.definition: A stereoscopic three-dimensional video is a video used to compare cybersickness severity on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets.

never_defined.name: flat screen
never_defined.definition: A flat screen is a display type used for viewing stereoscopic three-dimensional videos, and it is one of the display conditions compared with panoramic screens and VR headsets in cybersickness studies.

never_defined.name: panoramic screen
never_defined.definition: A panoramic screen is a type of display on which stereoscopic 3D videos can be viewed.

never_defined.name: brightness
never_defined.definition: Brightness is a display quality of head-mounted displays associated with cybersickness.

never_defined.name: clarity
never_defined.definition: Clarity is a display quality of a head-mounted display (HMD).

never_defined.name: contrast
never_defined.definition: Contrast is one of the display qualities of head-mounted displays.

never_defined.name: input method
never_defined.definition: Input method is a type of input used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, that can influence cybersickness.

never_defined.name: hand controller
never_defined.definition: A hand controller is one of the input methods used in virtual reality.

never_defined.name: motion sensor
never_defined.definition: A Motion sensor is an input method used in virtual reality and a miniaturized component that can be placed on augmented reality contact lenses.

never_defined.name: motion controller
never_defined.definition: A motion controller is a VR controller, such as steering with handlebars.

never_defined.name: joystick
never_defined.definition: A joystick is a non-motion, world-grounded hand input device that is fixed in the real world, is commonly used to interact with grounded systems, and is used to navigate or teleport.

never_defined.name: gamepad controller
never_defined.definition: A gamepad controller is a controller that causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

never_defined.name: input technology
never_defined.definition: Input technology is a hardware factor among the external factors that cause cybersickness.

never_defined.name: content factor
never_defined.definition: A content factor is an external factor in the causes of cybersickness.
